## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so there is no signal about architecture so far. With the default recipe the budget gives only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 steps. That is very little for a task with 257 actions and exact-build success. My first guess is that sample count and update count matter most, so all three candidates use the same recipe: 2 PPO epochs, 128 envs and 16-step rollouts. That gives about 243k steps over about 118 updates. Candidate A changes only the recipe and is the control. The structure of the task points to one key decision: a brick lands at the maximum build height under its footprint, and it is correct only if every footprint cell at that layer is missing from the build and no missing cell below gets sealed. Pooling max, min and average side by side cannot express this nested check (max, then a per-cell check, then min). Candidates B and C build that check into the head, in two different ways.

### Round 2
All four trials, the starting network and three round-1 variants, scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 in training success. That includes about 1.8x more steps (r1c1) and two richer footprint heads (r1c2, r1c3). The failure looks systematic, not a small gap a better head could close. Three explanations fit: (1) far too few samples and updates for exact builds and for learning DONE; (2) the world differs from the description, for example the action-to-cell mapping does not line up with the conv feature grid, which would break any position-aligned head; (3) the receptive field or the information is too limited. This round each candidate bundles changes so we are more likely to get any nonzero signal: a recipe with as many samples as possible (C2), the same recipe plus a head whose action layout is learned and global attention (C1), and the same recipe plus mask-as-input, a dilated trunk and skip features (C3). C1 and C3 can each be compared with C2.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success was also 0. The changes covered recipes from about 130k to 410k steps, three different footprint heads, attention, mask inputs and a wider receptive field. Seed noise cannot explain zero on every one. A sensible greedy policy should still build some 6-brick designs exactly, so I suspect a structural mismatch. The task notes the world may differ from its description. Likely culprits are the action layout (transposed or flipped axes, a different anchor corner, a different brick-type order), or obs and actions not lining up spatially. Every head so far assumes a top-left anchor and logits laid out by type, then y, then x. The 1x1 stem already absorbs any reordering of input channels. Steps are already near the maximum allowed (about 426k), so more samples won't help. This round I test heads that do not assume a layout: dense, dihedral and pure-MLP heads. All three use the legal-action mask, which is always given in the true action order.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0, both on dev and on training success. That covers bigger heads, layer-wise heads, attention, the mask as input, layout-agnostic dense heads, a pure MLP, and recipes giving up to about 426k steps. Since even the layout-free MLP never succeeds while sampling during training, an action-layout twist alone probably does not explain it. A likely shared failure is that learning collapses. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they earn negative reward, while DONE returns exactly 0. The policy can learn to stop early and then stop exploring before it can tell which placements are good. Every trial used lr 1e-3, default initialisation and entropy of 0.01 or less. Untested so far: stronger entropy, lower learning rate, normalised trunks, and near-uniform starting policies. With one round left, I put all three candidates on exploration and optimisation rather than layout.
